source_text: Id si dubitas, evolve quae spiritus ecclesiis dicat. Desertam dilectionem Ephesiis imputat, stuprum et idolothytorum esum Thyatirenis exprobrat, Sardos non plenorum operum incusat, Pergamenos docentes perversa reprehendit, Laodicenos fidentes divitiis obiurgat, et tamen omnes ad paenitentiam commonet, sub comminationibus quidem. Non comminaretur autem non paenitenti, si non ignosceret paenitenti. Dubium, si non et alibi hanc clementiae suae profusionem demonstrasset. Non ait, Qui ceciderit, resurget, et qui aversatus fuerit, convertetur? Ille est scilicet, ille est qui misericordiam mavult quam sacrificia. Laetantur caeli, et qui illic angeli, paenitentia hominis. Heus tu, peccator, bono animo sis! vides, ubi de tuo reditu gaudeatur. Quid illa similitudinum dominicarum argumenta nobis volunt? Quod mulier drachmam perdidit et requirit et reperit et amicas ad gaudium invitat, nonne restituti peccatoris exemplum est? Errat et una pastoris ovicula, sed grex una carior non erat: una illa conquiritur, una pro omnibus desideratur, et tandem invenitur et humeris pastoris ipsius refertur; multum enim errando laboraverat. Illum etiam mitissimum patrem non tacebo, qui prodigum filium revocat, et post inopiam paenitentem libens suscipit, immolat vitulum praeopimum, convivio gaudium suum exornat. Quidni? filium enim invenerat quem amiserat, cariorem senserat quem lucri fecerat. Quis ille nobis intellegendus pater? Deus scilicet. Tam pater nemo, tam pius nemo. Is ergo te filium suum, etsi acceptum ab eo prodegeris, etsi nudus redieris, recipiet, quia redisti, magisque de regressu tuo quam de alterius sobrietate laetabitur; sed si paeniteat ex animo, si famem tuam cum saturitate mercenariorum paternorum compares, si porcos immundum relinquas pecus, si patrem repetas vel offensum, Deliqui, dicens, pater, nec dignus ego iam vocari tuus. Tantum relevat confessio delictorum, quantum dissimulatio exaggerat. Confessio enim satisfactionis consilium est, dissimulatio contumaciae.
thought_title: God's mercy shown in Scripture and parables
orientation: Tertullian is urging a sinner not to doubt God's willingness to forgive a second repentance, and now turns to Scripture and the parables of Jesus as proof of God's mercy.
pass_a_gloss: If you doubt this, unroll what the Spirit says to the churches. He charges the Ephesians with abandoned love, he reproaches the Thyatirenes for fornication and eating of idol-sacrifices, he accuses the Sardians of not having complete works, he rebukes the Pergamenes for teaching perverse things, he scolds the Laodiceans for trusting in riches, and yet he urges all to repentance, under threats indeed. But he would not threaten the one not repenting, if he did not forgive the one repenting. It would be doubtful, if he had not also elsewhere shown this outpouring of his mercy. Does he not say, He who has fallen will rise again, and he who has turned away will be converted? He is of course, he is the one who prefers mercy rather than sacrifices. The heavens rejoice, and the angels who are there, at the repentance of a human. Hey you, sinner, be of good cheer! You see where there is rejoicing over your return. What do those arguments of the Lord's parables want for us? That a woman lost a drachma and seeks it and finds it and invites her friends to joy, is it not an example of the restored sinner? Also one little sheep of the shepherd wanders, but the one flock was not dearer: that one is sought out, that one is longed for in place of all, and at last it is found and is carried back on the shoulders of the shepherd himself; for it had labored much by wandering. I will not be silent also about that most gentle father, who calls back his prodigal son, and after poverty receives him willingly as he repents, sacrifices a very fat calf, adorns his joy with a feast. Why not? For he had found the son whom he had lost, he had felt him dearer whom he had made a gain. Who is that father to be understood by us as? God of course. No one is so much a father, no one is so pious. Therefore he will receive you, his son, even if you have squandered what you received from him, even if you return naked, because you have returned, and he will rejoice more over your return than over the sobriety of another; but only if you repent from the heart, if you compare your hunger with the fullness of your father's hired servants, if you leave the pigs, the unclean herd, if you seek your father again even though offended, saying, I have sinned, father, and I am no longer worthy to be called yours. Confession of sins relieves as much as concealment exaggerates. For confession is the counsel of making amends, concealment is the counsel of defiance.

choices.why: Glossary term; the divinely appointed discipline of turning from sin.
Keeps the participial force of the Latin, showing the person engaged in the act of repentance.
Delictum is the glossary term for sin; confession here is the act that leads to making amends.
Glossary term; the making of amends to God through confession and penitential discipline.
Glossary term; defiant disobedience, the attitude of one who conceals sin.
Captures the direct, encouraging address to the sinner; idiomatic English for the Latin phrase.

pass_b_english: If you doubt this, look at what the Spirit says to the churches. He charges the church in Ephesus with abandoning its first love. He rebukes the church in Thyatira for fornication and eating food sacrificed to idols. He accuses the church in Sardis of incomplete works. He reproaches the church in Pergamum for teaching falsehood. He scolds the church in Laodicea for trusting in riches. Yet he urges them all to repentance, though with threats. He would not threaten the one who refuses to repent if he did not forgive the one who repents. Could there be any doubt, when he has shown this outpouring of his mercy elsewhere as well? Does he not say, "The one who falls will rise again, and the one who turns away will turn back"? He is the one, surely, who desires mercy rather than sacrifices. The heavens rejoice, and the angels there, over the repentance of a human being. So be of good cheer, you sinner! You see where your return brings joy.

What do those parables of the Lord mean for us? A woman loses a coin, searches for it, finds it, and invites her friends to celebrate. Is that not a picture of the restored sinner? One little sheep of the shepherd's wanders off, but the flock as a whole was not dearer to him. That one is sought out, that one is longed for more than all the rest, and at last it is found and carried back on the shepherd's own shoulders. It had suffered much in its wandering.

I will not pass over that most gentle father either, who calls back his prodigal son, and after his poverty welcomes him gladly when he repents. He slaughters the fattened calf and adorns his joy with a feast. Why not? He had found the son he had lost, and felt him dearer because he had gained him back. Who is this father we are to understand? God, of course. No one is so much a father, no one so loving. He will receive you as his son, even if you have squandered what he gave you, even if you return naked, because you have returned. He will rejoice more over your coming back than over the sobriety of another. But only if you repent from the heart, if you compare your hunger with the fullness of your father's hired servants, if you leave the pigs, that unclean herd, if you seek your father again even though you have offended him, saying, "Father, I have sinned, and I am no longer worthy to be called yours." Confession of sins brings as much relief as concealment adds weight. For confession is the plan for making amends; concealment is defiance.
